messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Ravi is a 29-year-old South Asian man who recently sought help for persistent anxiety and distress following a traumatic mugging. A painter by profession, Ravi has been struggling with his daily routine since the incident occurred about six months ago. The mugging happened while he was returning home late one evening after completing an urgent painting job at a local gallery. As he walked through a dimly lit alley near his apartment building, he was suddenly confronted by three men who demanded his wallet and phone. In the ensuing struggle, Ravi sustained minor injuries but managed to escape. Since that night, Ravi has been experiencing vivid nightmares where he relives the traumatic event. Every time he wakes up from these dreams, he feels a sudden surge of fear and anger, leaving him irritable and tense throughout the day. His body remains on high alert, constantly scanning his surroundings for any signs of danger. Even mundane tasks like walking to his car or returning home from work can trigger intense feelings of unease. Ravi's memories of the mugging are fragmented and incomplete, often surfacing unexpectedly at seemingly random moments. These intrusive recollections are accompanied by a deep sense of guilt, as he wonders if he could have done more to prevent the incident. When he tries to deliberately recall what happened, his mind goes blank, leaving him with a frustrating feeling that crucial details are missing. Ravi’s experience has led him to develop a profound mistrust towards others. He believes that people cannot be trusted and feels deeply isolated from those around him, including his wife. This sense of isolation is compounded by the belief that he can’t rely on anyone else for support or protection. These negative beliefs have made it difficult for Ravi to engage in social activities, leading him to avoid places where he might encounter crowds or reminders of the mugging. The more Ravi feels isolated and mistrustful, the more his body remains tense and alert, perpetuating a cycle of heightened anxiety. His constant scanning for danger is not just a physical response but also a mental one, as thoughts about potential threats dominate his mind. This hyper-vigilance has made it increasingly difficult for him to concentrate on his work, leading to delays in completing projects and even occasional arguments with clients. Ravi’s avoidance behaviors have taken a toll on both his personal relationships and professional life. He avoids walking through the same alley where he was mugged and generally tries to stay away from any location that reminds him of the traumatic event. His wife has noticed these changes, but Ravi finds it hard to confide in her about his fears and guilt. The combination of these symptoms has left Ravi feeling overwhelmed and isolated. He has finally decided to seek help after realizing that his fear and mistrust were affecting his ability to function at work and maintain a healthy relationship with his wife. What frightens him most is the prospect of never being able to shake off the constant sense of danger and guilt. He hopes that through therapy, he can regain control over his life and find ways to trust others again without reliving the trauma every day.
